analysis.title: AI and credit: Looking beyond the technology race
key_insights: Central argument: for a credit investor, who wins the financing arms race matters more than who wins the AI race. Much of the debt being raised is better viewed through an infrastructure lens than as a binary call on the technology.

The five major hyperscalers (Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle) issued $240.7B of debt year-to-date as of 31 August, $66B of it in non-dollar currencies. Adding USD issuance from SpaceX and Nvidia brings combined issuance to $290.7B across currencies (source cited: Morgan Stanley, August 2026).

Technology is about 11% of the Bloomberg US Corporate IG index but a much larger share of new issuance. Excess spread on the technology sector over the broad index has widened materially since the build-out began, while spreads outside technology and its adjacencies have kept tightening.

Hyperscalers are at 1.2-1.4% index weights as of July, including off-balance sheet data centre financing. JP Morgan data shows large issuers routinely held 3-8% of the US IG corporates index before 2008, so Capital Group sees substantial headroom.

Hyperscaler metrics are deteriorating from a strong base (JP Morgan, 14 July 2026): gross leverage 1.8x (+26% y/y) vs 3.3x (+1%) for IG ex-hyperscalers, EBITDA margin 41% vs 32%, interest coverage 56.2x (-36%) vs 8.8x (-1%).

Capital Group's working view is that the market can keep absorbing supply while the economy stays healthy, fundamentals stay strong and yield demand persists, at the cost of ongoing technical pressure and periodic indigestion.

Watch items: early signs of AI issuance fatigue (a high yield data centre financing was postponed and restructured after weak demand, and enthusiasm for recent deals is less uniform), a fall in demand for yield if yields drop below a threshold, and capex growing faster than cash flow for a prolonged period.

Credit investors need to assess whether an issuer can fund the investment and keep meeting obligations across outcomes. Cash flow certainty is highest near physical inputs (compute, power, infrastructure) and lowest at the model and application layers, where outcomes are more binary.

Because credit upside is capped at yield plus par, the infrastructure layer with hard asset backing and contracted cash flow is seen as the more attractive layer. The model and application layers carry terminal value and default risk.

SPV-based data centre financings with a hyperscaler backstop trade at a yield pick-up to the parent. The main risks are delivery (site, construction, power delays) and durability (tenant quality, whether residual value guarantees are enforceable). Risk fades as the data centre comes online, which can catalyse spread tightening.

Beignet Investor LLC, a Blue Owl Capital vehicle funding a 2.1-gigawatt Meta data centre campus in Louisiana, holds the largest single-tranche bond in the US IG market. The bonds are not index-eligible but are very liquid.

Four scenarios through 2033 (capacity glut, build and they come, seller's market, AI hangover). Credit and equity outcomes can diverge: weaker AI demand could cut hyperscaler capex and support their free cash flow and spreads, while strong demand could sustain heavy issuance and technical pressure.

Software has been a cautionary tale for AI disruption. Capital Group estimates 15-25% of leveraged loans and direct lending is loans to software companies, against 2-3% of public high yield and IG indices. The 2020/21 vintage of loans nears maturity at much higher financing costs, which could mean private credit write-downs.

Portfolio positioning: modest, selective overweight to hyperscalers and IG data centres, a preference for select industrial suppliers (power generation, infrastructure equipment), less exposure to semiconductor issuers that take on balance sheet risk to finance customers' chip purchases, and gradual scaling into positions.

sector_views.rationale: Modest, selective overweight. Strong operating cash flow and balance sheets, with selectivity among issuers and SPV structures.
Benefit from AI infrastructure demand without the same financing and contingent-liability risk as hyperscalers.
Less exposure where companies take on additional balance sheet risk to facilitate customers' chip purchases.

sector_views.sector: Software (leveraged loans, direct lending, high yield)
sector_views.rationale: Investors are re-pricing terminal value for lower quality software borrowers, and older loans face higher refinancing costs.

trade_ideas.description: Modest, selective overweight to hyperscaler and investment-grade data centre bonds, scaling in gradually
trade_ideas.rationale: Companies can generate meaningful AI-related revenue while balancing the risk of continued heavy debt issuance, and indigestion creates better entry points.
trade_ideas.risk: Heavy continued issuance, capex outgrowing cash flow, and SPV structures whose backstops may not be enforceable.

trade_ideas.description: Overweight select industrial suppliers (power generation and infrastructure equipment) credit
trade_ideas.rationale: They benefit from AI infrastructure demand without the same financing and contingent-liability risk as hyperscalers.

risk_factors: AI issuance fatigue: less uniform demand for recent deals and a postponed, restructured high yield data centre financing.
Demand for yield could fall away if yields drop below a certain threshold, removing a technical support.
Capex growing faster than cash flow for a prolonged period could pressure leverage metrics and investor confidence.
Rating downgrade risk from large-scale issuance raising leverage.
SPV structure risk: construction delays, lease termination provisions and asset value if the tenant walks away.
Terminal value risk and potential defaults in the model and application layers.
Private credit and leveraged loan write-downs on software loans from the 2020/21 vintage.
vol_and_positioning: Spread technicals: hyperscaler spreads have widened since large-scale issuance began and pressure may continue until supply stabilises. The report expects periods of indigestion and greater valuation dispersion, which would create better entry points.

tension_points.bull_case: Strong hyperscaler balance sheets and contracted infrastructure cash flows can support credit even if AI investment accelerates. Spreads on the highest-quality credits may tighten if AI demand disappoints and capex is cut.
tension_points.bear_case: Heavier issuance creates technical pressure, early signs of issuance fatigue have appeared, and capex growing faster than cash flow could strain leverage and investor confidence.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Capex continuing to grow faster than cash flow generation for a prolonged period, or yields falling below the threshold at which new buyers stop buying credit.
